events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.description: Worth Ryder Art Gallery and the VIDRINE present four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light's BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels.Featured Artworks: Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner — AnointedMichael Light — BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023Michael Pinsky — MammothDavid Buckland �� Bikini TextsAbout Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley (http://ourlifeishere.org)In 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with Marshallese youth and elders. This expedition—organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, with support from Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell—was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. Throughout 2026–27, the project runs across campus in exhibitions at Doe Library, Giannini Hall, Memorial Glade, Worth Ryder, and BAMPFA, along with courses and public programs. It culminates in an exhibition of original works at the David Brower Center, September 2027 – February 2028. ourlifeishere.org (https://art.berkeley.edu/ourlifeishere.org)About Worth Ryder Art Gallery / VIDRINE (https://art.berkeley.edu/gallery)The Worth Ryder Art Gallery (WRAG) is an educational art space that has served as a cultural and artistic resource and community center for undergraduate and graduate students, faculty, alumni, and the Bay Area community since 1960, and is a central social and artistic hub of the UC Berkeley Department of Art Practice. The gallery supports students in exhibiting their artwork in a professional gallery context, serves as an exhibition platform for emerging contemporary artistic strategies, and brings challenging and thought-provoking artwork to the UC Berkeley campus. It is named after painter and founding chair of the department, Worth Ryder. VIDRINE is Worth Ryder Art Gallery's ancillary space showcasing video, digital art, and installation. It is located around the corner from the Worth Ryder Art Gallery in the lobby of the Anthropology and Art Building.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. events.description: Harunobu Mitsunuma, Associate professor, Kobe UniversityDevelopment of catalyst systems enabling sp3 C‒H functionalization reactionsDr. Mitsunuma has made pioneering contributions to catalytic sp³ C–H activation through his development of a cooperative catalyst system in which distinct catalysts operate synergistically. This strategy enabled mild sp³ C–H functionalization that combines high stereocontrol with high functional group compatibility. In particular, his ternary catalytic platform integrating a hydrogen atom transfer catalyst, a metal complex catalyst, and a photoredox catalyst has realized unprecedented transformations, including nucleophilic addition reactions in which simple hydrocarbons serve directly as nucleophiles, as well as highly mild catalytic acceptorless dehydrogenation. Dr. Harunobu Mitsunuma received his Ph.D. from the University of Tokyo in 2015 under the supervision of Professor Motomu Kanai. He subsequently worked as a medicinal chemist at Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma, contributing to early-stage drug discovery. In 2017, he returned to academia as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Tokyo and was promoted to appointed assistant professor in 2018. Since 2022, he has also served concurrently as a PRESTO researcher, further advancing his research program. In 2026, he was appointed as an independent associate professor at the Graduate School of Science, Kobe University.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Risk Appetite and Monetary Transmission"
events.description: Abstract: We construct a new high-frequency measure of risk appetite shifts around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings, the common component of changes in risk-sensitive indicators. Fed policy actions and communication have substantial effects on risk appetite. Interest-rate surprises explain only about one-fifth of the variation in risk appetite, so most policy-induced changes in risk asset prices are orthogonal to the expected rate path. We therefore use both surprises as external instruments in a proxy SVAR with two separately identified shocks. Risk appetite shocks have large and persistent contractionary effects, lowering output and prices while raising unemployment. By contrast, the effects of risk-free rate shocks tend to be small and imprecisely estimated, and some have puzzling signs. Monetary transmission appears to operate primarily through risk appetite and risk asset prices. Estimates relying on interest-rate surprises alone miss most of these effects, for two reasons: the link from interest rates to risk appetite is state-dependent, and Fed communication moves it independently of the expected rate path.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics: Cary Frydman "On the Source and Instability of Probability Weighting"
events.description: Abstract: We propose and experimentally test a new theory of probability distortions in risky choice. Thetheory is based on a core principle from neuroscience called efficient coding, which states that information is encoded more accurately for those stimuli that the agent expects to encounter morefrequently. As the agent's prior beliefs vary, the model predicts that probability distortions changesystematically. We provide novel experimental evidence consistent with this prediction by manipulating and measuring a subject's prior beliefs. The data reveal that lottery valuations are moresensitive to probabilities that occur more frequently under the subject's reported prior beliefs. events.title: Topology Seminar: Instantons and the Dehn surgery number
events.description: Speaker: Ali Daemi, Washington University in St. LouisEvery closed oriented 3-manifold can be obtained by Dehn surgery on a link in the 3-sphere. The minimum number of components of such a link is called the Dehn surgery number of the 3-manifold. Although it is a natural measure of the complexity of 3-manifolds, the Dehn surgery number is difficult to compute. In this talk, I will discuss a result based on join work with Xingpei Liu and Mike Miller Eismeier in which we show that integer homology spheres can have arbitrarily large Dehn surgery numbers, resolving a question of Auckly. Our approach uses an invariant introduced by Frøyshov, defined in terms of mod 2 instanton Floer homology. We establish new constraints on how this invariant behaves under 4-dimensional cobordisms, leading to lower bounds on Dehn surgery numbers.

events.title: Operator Algebras Seminar: Nonisomorphism of q-Gaussian algebras in infinite variables
events.description: Speaker: Zhiyuan Yang, Purdue UniversityThe q-Gaussian von Neumann algebras, introduced by Bożejko and Speicher, form a family of II_1 factors that deform Voiculescu's free Gaussian factors. For finitely many variables, Guionnet and Shlyakhtenko showed that small deformations do not change the isomorphism class. We focus on the case of infinitely many variables.Previous work of Borst, Caspers, Klisse, and Wasilewski showed that the corresponding C*-algebras A_q and A_0 are not isomorphic for q nonzero, using the failure of the Akemann-Ostrand property (AO). Caspers later established the corresponding result for the von Neumann algebras M_q. We show more generally that M_q is isomorphic to M_r if and only if q=r, which also implies the same result for A_q and A_r.The proof is based on a closer study of the kernel of the Akemann-Ostrand map. We show that this kernel has a natural filtration by ideals. In particular, its least noncompact ideal contains the projection onto the first chaos of the q-Fock space. This property allows us to recover the parameter q intrinsically from the von Neumann algebra and therefore shows the nonisomorphism.

events.title: Student Harmonic Analysis and PDE Seminar (HADES): Initial Data Gluing for Asymptotically Hyperbolic Spacetimes
events.description: Speaker: Aren Martinian, UC BerkeleyGluing techniques in general relativity are incredibly versatile, for example in combining multiple gravitational systems together or improving understanding of black hole initial data. Such gluing constructions have been done in a wide variety of settings, including those of constant nonzero curvature. In this talk, we give a new proof of Corvino-Schoen type gluing, also known as gluing up to linear obstructions, for asymptotically hyperbolic spacetimes satisfying improved quantitative smallness conditions in arbitrary dimension over the existing work of Chruściel and Delay, also generalizing this work to the non-time-symmetric case k ≠ 0. In particular, we describe three Bogovskii solution operators, inspired by the framework of Mao-Oh-Tao, with each providing a distinct and important role in the construction.

events.title: Joint Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics and Seminar PHDBA 239S Finance: "The Optimal Use of AI in Financial Regulation"
events.description: Abstract: We study whether AI methods applied to large-scale portfolio holdings data can improve financial stability monitoring and inform macroprudential regulation. We build a graph-based deep learning model tailored to security-level data on the holdings of financial intermediaries. The architecture incorporates economic priors and learns latent representations of both assets and investors from the network structure of portfolio positions. Applied to the universe of non-bank financial intermediaries, covering nearly $40 trillion in wealth, the model substantially outperforms a broad set of existing approaches in out-of-sample forecasts of intermediary trading behavior, including in crisis episodes. The model's incremental explanatory power for the cross-section of asset returns during stress events is more than ten times that of traditional holdings based approaches, and it outperforms existing systemic risk metrics at the institution level. Its learned representations show that the holdings network encodes rich, economically interpretable information about fire-sale vulnerability. The model is inductive, producing informative estimates also for unseen assets and investors. We embed ourempirical approach into a macroprudential optimal policy framework to formalize why these objects matter for policy and welfare. We characterize when the predictive information from the model improves welfare by sharpening the cross-sectional targeting of policy interventions, and we demonstrate a complementarity between prediction and structural knowledge.

events.title: Two Concepts of Patriotism: Nationalist and Civic
events.description: REGISTER Register to join us on October 20 for a Matrix Teach-In by Desmond Jagmohan, Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley. The Matrix Teach-In series (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/matrix-teach-in/) brings some of UC Berkeley's most engaging social science lecturers into a public setting. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Charles and Louise Travers Department of Political Science.Abstract This lecture distinguishes nationalist from civic patriotism. Donald Trump has voiced the former as a summons to restore a lost greatness, Barack Obama the latter as a call to fulfill the unkept promise of the Declaration of Independence, an ideal not yet fully realized. The lecture argues that civic patriotism offers the nobler and more democratic vision, but that a civic patriotism adequate to our moment must also take seriously the lost standing of working-class Americans, those whose material precarity, and the attenuation that follows, draws them to nationalist patriotism. Liberals must do more than reclaim the symbols of patriotism in the name of realizing political and social equality; they should also pursue an economic nationalism that puts Americans first, one that recognizes that, in America, earning determines standing.About the SpeakerDesmond Jagmohan (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/desmond-jagmohan) is Assistant Professor of Political Science at the University of California, Berkeley. He specializes in the history of American and African American political thought, American intellectual history, and the history of political thought. His research concerns political and moral agency under conditions of extreme oppression. He is completing his first book, Dark Virtues: Booker T. Washington's Tragic Realism (under contract with Princeton University Press), which draws on several years of archival research to recover Washington as a virtue theorist of the oppressed. His second book will read Harriet Jacobs's slave narrative as a work of moral and political theory that grounds the wrong of slavery in property rights in another person. His work has been published in Journal of Politics, Political Theory, Annual Review of Political Science, Perspectives on Politics, Politics, Groups, and Identities, Contemporary Political Theory, and Boston Review. Professor Jagmohan is the winner of several awards and fellowships: The APSA Best Dissertation Award from the Race, Ethnicity and Politics Section (2015), a National Fellow at the Hoover Institution, Stanford University (2018), and a Laurance S. Rockefeller Visiting Faculty Fellow at University Center for Human Values at Princeton University, and Hellman Fellowship at UC, Berkeley. Prior to arriving at Berkeley, he was Assistant Professor of Politics at Princeton University, where he delivered the 2018 Constitution Day Lecture and was awarded the Laurance S. Rockefeller University Preceptorship in the University Center for Human Values. He holds an M.A. and a Ph.D. from Cornell University.

events.title: Jürgen Dinkel | All remains in the Family: A History of Inheritance in the US and Europe Since 1800
events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025). events.title: Poetry Event for César Vallejo's TRILCE: A New English Translation
events.description: Reading/Discussion w/Translators William Rowe and Helen Dimos, in conversation with Professors Estelle Tarica (Chair, Spanish & Portuguese, UC Berkeley), Victor Quiroz (Modern Languages & Literatures, Santa Clara University), and Robert Kaufman (Comparative Literature; Program in Critical Theory; UC Berkeley) This year, New York Review Books published a new translation into English of the renowned Peruvian poet César Vallejo's groundbreaking work Trilce (1922). Initially denounced as an impossibly obtuse work, the volume of linked poems stretched the limits of language and eventually became known as a signal-work of poetic art, widely considered to have spurred key developments in later modern and avant-gardist poetry worldwide.NYRB's new bilingual edition of TRILCE includes glosses by translators WILLIAM ROWE and HELEN DIMOS, giving readers a deeper look into these fascinating poems, as well as at the artist and social dynamics behind and inside them.TRILCE transformed poetry in Spanish utterly, remaking the substance and forms of verse from phoneme and word on up. Rich in startling neologisms and other forms of verbal play, TRILCE is a blazingly vivid revelation of what poetry can be: at once a love poem, a poem of erotic urgency and frustration, family life, political fury; a lament for the dead; a work of intense privacy; an address to the world. As a whole, the work constitutes a profound reckoning with time—the time of literary forms and their conjunctions with social and political time; the time of Indigenous and traditional cultural forms–all of which work together to create a new poetic now. Haunting and incantatory, Vallejo's complex set of poems speaks powerfully to us, as we in our time seek to find what needs to be made present. In this new bilingual edition of Trilce —recipient of the prestigious Premio Valle Inclán for the best translation of a literary work from from Spanish into English—the translators Helen Dimos and William Rowe, celebrated poets themselves, accompany each poem with a gloss. Their incisive commentary on these legendarily challenging poems opens them to new understanding while inviting readers to find their own pathways to and through them.

events.title: Conversations on AI: Beyond Code at Cal
events.description: As AI reshapes every industry, what does a real pathway into tech look like for the people traditional education has left behind? Part 1 — Panel: Introducing Beyond Code Collective A moderated panel that introduces Beyond Code Collective to the Berkeley community—the why behind its founding, the model, and the cohort tracks that make it different from any other workforce program on the market today. THEMES FOR THE CONVERSATION • The founding story — Cristina Mancini's path from leading Black Girls Code to launching Beyond Code Collective. Why the moment demanded a new organization—one built explicitly to serve everyone, from teenagers to career pivoters to retiring athletes. • From Black Girls Code to Beyond Code — What was learned from more than a decade of building an inclusive tech education model, and how those lessons translate into a program designed for a much broader audience. • The cohort model in practice — Beyond Code Catalysts, After The Game, and the emerging industry-specific tracks (athletics, construction, and others). What does a cohort actually look like, and why is that structure the right answer for AI-era workforce development? • Re-educating a workforce, not replacing it — The framing that AI eliminates jobs misses the real story—which is that every job is being rewritten. How does Beyond Code think about upskilling, credentialing (CompTIA, Salesforce, AWS), and the wraparound support that makes retraining actually stick? • The role of community and place — The Forge model as a "third space" outside traditional schools and workplaces. What would it mean to bring that model, even temporarily, to a campus like Berkeley? • What Berkeley can do — A direct call to the audience: how alumni, students, faculty, and employer partners in the room can plug in—as learners, mentors, hiring partners, or funders. Part 2 — Hands-On Training Immediately following the panel, the Beyond Code team leads a hands-on training session for attendees who want to move from inspired to enrolled.

events.description: From the Ground Up follows artist Leon Sun, historians Barnali Ghosh and Anirvan Chatterjee of the Berkeley South Asian Radical History Walking Tour (https://www.berkeleysouthasian.org/), and Caroline Cabading of Manilatown Heritage Foundation (https://www.manilatown.org/) as they explore the intersections of Asian American community art, history, and archival work in the San Francisco Bay Area. The Berkeley South Asian Radical History Walking Tour (berkeleysouthasian.org (https://www.berkeleysouthasian.org/)) has been educating the public on the local history of South Asian Americans since 2012. Their popular 3-hour tours provide "a deeply researched, sometimes emotional, and always inspiring glimpse at four generations of Desi freedom fighters, feminists, students, queer activists, and more". Check out their website for some amazing local history resources, like the Secret Desi History blog (secretdesihistory.com (https://www.secretdesihistory.com/)).From the Ground Up also profiles the activists behind the Manilatown Heritage Foundation, (https://www.manilatown.org/) whose mission is to promote social and economic justice for Filipinos in the United States by preserving history, advocating for equal access, and advancing Filipino arts and culture. They operate the International Hotel Manilatown Center, "the historic site of the community struggle to save the International Hotel and prevent the eviction of its elderly residents from 1968-1977. [The I-Hotel] became a focal point in the creation of the contemporary Asian American movement, especially for Filipino Americans and San Francisco's housing justice movement" (from https://www.manilatown.org/international-hotel-manilatown-center (https://www.manilatown.org/international-hotel-manilatown-center)).

events.title: Matthew Carlson // Future Farming: Designing Start-ups in a Big Company
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Matthew Carlson, Director of Product Design for Aqua at Adobe, an internal start-up focused on creativity tools for kids. With a career spanning Adobe, Twitter, and Meta, Matthew specializes in building and scaling internal start-ups within large organizations, creating products that explore new opportunities while navigating complex systems. His work sits at the intersection of product design, creativity, and emerging technologies, with a focus on empowering the next generation of creators. ​In this talk, Matthew will explore how innovation takes root inside large organizations, where ideas grow toward opportunity much like plants toward sunlight. events.title: The Computer in the Sky
events.description: Turing-complete blockchain protocols such as Ethereum approximate the idealized abstraction of a shared "computer in the sky" by augmenting the traditional internet with persistent-state and processing capabilities. This technology can, among other things, enable stronger notions of ownership of digital possessions than we have ever had before. Building the computer in the sky is hard (and scientifically fascinating), and requires the synthesis of multiple disciplines, both within computer science (distributed computing, cryptography, algorithmic game theory) and beyond (mechanism design, macroeconomics, finance, political science). This talk will survey some of Tim Roughgarden's work in the area and the practical impact it has had.Tim Roughgarden is a Professor in the School of Mathematics at the Institute for Advanced Study, on leave from the Department of Computer Science at Columbia University. He is also the Founding Head of Research at a16z crypto. Prior to joining Columbia, he spent 15 years on the computer science faculty at Stanford, following a PhD at Cornell and a postdoc at UC Berkeley. He works on the boundary of computer science and economics, and on the design, analysis, applications, and limitations of algorithms. _______________________Theoretically Speaking is a lecture series highlighting exciting advances in theoretical computer science for a broad general audience. Events are free and open to the public, with first-come, first-served seating. No special background is assumed. Registration is required. This lecture will be viewable afterward on this page and on our YouTube channel (https://www.youtube.com/user/SimonsInstitute), following captioning.Light refreshments will be provided before the talk, starting at 5 p.m.The Simons Institute regularly captures photos and video of activity around the Institute for use in publications and promotional materials.

events.title: Bereza/Beryoze: Old Ukrainian and Yiddish songs in a new song cycle from Zozulka Trio
events.location: Wu Performance Hall, Department of Music, UC Berkeley
events.description: 6:30pm Doors, 7:00pm PerformanceFree and open to the public Many old songs brim with ecological awareness. Songs from the territory of modern Ukraine tell stories about plants like the birch tree–bereza in Ukrainian, beryoze in Yiddish–that bend, break, and heal, becoming metaphors for human fragility and tenacity. Birds mark the turning of seasons and shifts in our internal weather as well. Since 2011, Zozulka (https://zozulka.bandcamp.com/track/war-song)—a trio named after the Ukrainian word for cuckoo bird—has interpreted songs from a wide range of Ukrainian village traditions. With BEREZA / BERYOZE, the trio branches into a new cycle of songs that speak directly to ecological themes. In this project, Zozulka reaches into Yiddish song repertoires from Ukraine, matching and contrasting the Jewish and Ukrainian song traditions that coexisted and drew upon grounded ecological knowledge. This song cycle reimagines old songs by rooting them in new sonic and cultural landscapes. Through expansive and bold arrangements, the works in BEREZA / BERYOZE illuminate how folk wisdom can deepen our awareness of the interdependence between human and more-than-human worlds. In an era marked by global climate change and devastating acts of ecocide in wartorn Ukraine and beyond, BEREZA / BERYOZE celebrates variegated and interlinked song traditions and the cathartic, regenerative power of singing old songs in the present. The performance will be followed by a talk-back between the group and the audience, joined by joined by scholar and visual artist Darya Tsymbalyuk (https://artshumanities.uchicago.edu/directory/darya-tsymbalyuk) (University of Chicago), moderated by Nataliia Goshylyk (Lecturer in Ukrainian, Slavic Languages and Literatures).Zozulka Trio is Eva Salina, Willa Roberts, and Maria Sonevytsky. They have been singing together since 2011, when they formed as an offshoot of The Chornobyl Songs Project, led the Kyiv-based ethnomusicologist Yevhen Yefremov. zozulka.bandcamp.com (https://zozulka.bandcamp.com/)Cosponsored by the Departments of Music, Slavic Languages and Literatures, and Center for Jewish Studies

events.title: Paloma Angelina Lopez and Abraham Matias | Popo the Xolo/Popo el xolo
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description: Event Description Join us for a live read-aloud of Popo the Xolo/Popo el xolo, the 2026 Américas Award winning picture book, with author Paloma Angelina Lopez and illustrator Abraham Matias. This event is designed for classrooms and is open to educators and librarians across the country.About the book Nana is surrounded by family and takes joy in her many grandchildren. She's also tired and feels pain. Soon she begins her transition from life into death, accompanied by her beloved Xolo dog, Popo. Together they go on Nana's journey, and by the end of the story, Nana's family celebrates the many years of love they shared with her. A grandchild takes on caring for Popo in Nana's memory. Simultaneously published in English and Spanish, Popo the Xolo helps kids understand how loved ones live on in our memories. An unforgettable picture book that's grounded in the importance of the 9 levels of Mictlān and the role Xolo dogs play in Indigenous cultural understandings of present-day Mexico.The event is hosted by the Américas Award in collaboration with Teaching for Change's Teaching Central America program. The Américas Award for Children's and Young Adult Literature was founded in 1993 by the Consortium of Latin American Studies Programs (CLASP), of which Berkeley CLACS is a member. The Award commends authors, illustrators, and publishers who produce quality children's and young adult books that portray Latin America, the Caribbean, or Latinos in the United States, and to provide teachers with recommendations for classroom use. CLASP offers up to two annual book awards, together with a commended list of titles. By linking the Americas, the intent is to reach beyond geographic borders, focusing instead upon cultural heritages within the hemisphere.Presented by theConsortium of Latin American Studies Programs, coordinated by Tulane University's Stone Center for Latin American Studies and Vanderbilt University's Center for Latin American, Caribbean, and Latinx Studies, and supported by Berkeley CLACS.

events.title: Meeting the Challenges of Transportation Liability and Risk Management
events.description: Description Transportation entities face conflicting and intersecting priorities - they must provide safe, efficient, equitable, multi-modal transportation projects while mitigating financial, legal and operational risk. Legal risk should be addressed by transportation entities early and often, not just after lawsuits have been filed. Employees and officials planning, designing, maintaining and operating their entity's transportation infrastructure need to understand the major legal principles governing roadway litigation. An understanding of the legal statutes, cases, principles and outcomes will help all transportation employees, from engineers, to planners, to maintenance crews understand how to conduct their operations to minimize or reduce legal risk. The intent of this course is to help transportation practitioners understand what claims can be brought against a transportation entity for crashes, how the lawyers representing those entities manage and defend those cases, and how the non-legal transportation professional can actively reduce or manage litigation risks using engineering judgment, proper documentation, and collaboration with legal and non-legal professionals. The training will cover legal concepts related to unsafe condition claims in California, investigation of collisions from a litigation perspective (vs. from a purely operational perspective), and will focus on tort liability litigation practices. This course will cover planning and design elements that provide context sensitive solutions based on the unique geometrics of a given facility while reducing legal risk through proper documentation and engineering judgment. We will discuss legal cases and court decisions that provide the framework for transportation entities to defend against unsafe condition cases. The various defenses available to the transportation entities will be covered, along with practical information for transportation employees to build into their workflow that minimize or reduce legal risk while allowing for creative, innovative design solutions for transportation infrastructure projects. Although the cases discussed will involve lawsuits resulting from highway design, the information provided will help civil engineers involved as witnesses in various types of litigation. Topics Include The course will provide transportation personnel with an understanding of the following:litigation process, including the legal concepts for unsafe condition claims the concept of joint and several liability the available defenses the need for early investigation in some collision cases and the process of providing information (called discovery) during a lawsuit various types of written discovery, oral testimony typically done in these cases, as well as the necessary preparation and assistance needed by employees involved in the litigation matters how to respond to questions from attorneys and become an effective witness in depositions and at trial how to prepare for deposition testimony (and the importance of doing so) how to testify in a trial interaction discussion and pointers on preparing for testimony dispositive motions that can end a case short of a jury several motions, including demurrers, motions to strike, motions for design immunity, and a trial on affirmative defenses explain these motions, and the non-legal transportation official's critical role in successful outcomes to these motions for transportation entities focus on emerging trends in transportation engineering that affect tort liability and risk management. This will include a history of safety programs federally and in California, including the Highway Safety Act, various spot programs, as well as the evolution of corridor safety programs, and the transitions with reactive/proactive safety operations challenges of innovative transportation initiatives when juxtaposed with the tort liability scheme in California What You Will Learn The intent of the course is to improve public agency practices to effectively manage and reduce tort liability. The following learning objectives are primary for this course:Understand the nature of roadway litigation against transportation entities Understand the litigation process in tort liability litigation Familiarize non-legal transportation personnel with the litigation process and their role in that process: Helping them to proactively manage or reduce liability, while Helping the legal team defend litigation matters effectively Help participants with the process of deposition and trial testimony by helping them understand how to approach witness testimony Address current trends in road liability litigation and how those trends can be positively or negatively affected by the transportation employee's work Use real world case examples to teach transportation employees how to use liability neutral documentation Understand the importance of balancing factors in addressing the needs of all road users Who Should Attend This course will benefit transportation professionals (engineers and planners) who work for consultants, cities, counties, and state agencies involved in designing roadway projects. This course is designed for individuals with some background and training in designing streets and intersections who are interested in learning more about tort liability and how it relates to the highway design process. The course may also be helpful to the staff of public agencies who are involved with street and roadway maintenance on a day-to-day basis.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Lisandro Claudio
events.description: In The Profligate Colonial (Cornell, 2025) Lisandro Claudio (South & Southeast Asian Studies) reveals how austerity, long before it became a buzzword of modern technocracy, was a tool of US empire. Austerity is often praised as prudence in hard times, a responsible response to crisis. In the Philippines today, it is treated as common sense, an unquestioned commitment to a strong currency, low inflation, and fiscal restraint. Claudio argues that this orthodoxy is in fact a colonial inheritance — a legacy of American rule that cast Filipinos as reckless spenders and imposed monetary discipline as a civilizing force. At the center of this logic is the "profligate colonial," a feminized, racialized figure who wastes public funds and so requires the steady hand of imperial governance. Focusing on key moments in Philippine economic history across the twentieth century, Claudio charts how austerity was first exported through empire, then domesticated in line with nationalist ambitions. He shows that generations of Filipino policymakers, central bankers, and intellectuals absorbed the lessons of American "money doctors," transforming what was a means to build a colonial state on the cheap into a postcolonial moral imperative. Austerity became not just policy, but an ideology that transcended political divides and reshaped the boundaries of the Philippine economic imagination.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Kaiwen Hou (CTML GSR)
events.description: The CTML Seminar Series continues on October 21st! Join us for an exciting talk on "A Nonrecursive Characterization of Universal Least Favorable Models for One-Step TMLE" led by CTML GSR Kaiwen Hou. This talk will take place from 12:00PM-1:00PM at Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401.Abstract: Targeted minimum loss-based estimation (TMLE) updates an initial estimate of the data-generating distribution by minimizing a loss over a parametric model whose loss-based score equals the efficient influence function (EIF), producing a plug-in estimator of the target estimand. A universal least favorable model (ULFM) satisfies this score condition throughout its parameter space, whereas a local least favorable model satisfies it only at zero fluctuation. The former permits a single loss-minimization step in targeting, yielding one-step TMLE; the latter generally requires iterative updates as in iterative TMLE. One-step TMLE can offer greater finite-sample robustness, particularly when data are sparse relative to the target estimand. However, conventional ULFM construction requires recursive evaluation of the EIF, which can be computationally demanding and accumulate numerical integration error. These challenges are especially pronounced when the EIF lacks a closed-form expression, as in some coarsening models. We develop a nonrecursive characterization of ULFMs that admits explicit solutions in some settings and implicit representations in others. This formulation supports parallel computation and facilitates verification of the conditions on the minimum-loss estimator required for semiparametric efficiency. We introduce a class of valid losses and characterize the corresponding ULFMs, providing a basis for deriving exact or approximate closed-form solutions. We illustrate the approach across several estimation problems. For the average treatment effect, it recovers familiar updates under squared error and logistic losses. For integrated density powers, it yields previously unknown explicit path representations. For the variance of the conditional treatment effect under squared error loss, it characterizes the evolution of the regression contrast through an efficiently solvable Volterra equation. We also derive an implicit ULFM equation for target estimands under coarsening at random. Together, these results extend the practical scope of one-step TMLE to settings in which recursive ULFM construction is computationally burdensome.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Mónica Caudillo: "Exposure to Community Violence and Reproductive Aging in Mexico"
events.description: Mónica Caudillo is an Associate Professor in the Sociology Department at the University of Maryland, College Park. She holds a PhD in Sociology from New York University and specializes in domestic and international research in family demography, reproductive, maternal, and infant health, mortality, and aging. A large part of her work focuses on the demographic and health consequences of disruptions to social contexts in the United States and Mexico. One of her lines of research investigates the relationship between the opioid epidemic and fertility, family formation, and family structures in the United States. Another set of projects assesses the effect of community violence on health and family formation and stability in Mexico. Her projects in this area of work focus on how outcomes such as union formation and dissolution, suicide, and reproductive and maternal health change during violent periods in that country. In addition, she is currently conducting work on how exposure to community violence shapes different dimensions of aging, such as cognitive decline and reproductive aging, and the latter's implications for broader demographic trends in Mexico and the United States.

events.title: Mass Democratic Politics as Spectator Sport: A Historical Perspective | History Department Colloquium - David Henkin
events.description: Please save the date for the History Department's second Faculty Colloquium of the year with David Henkin, Professor of History. "Mass Democratic Politics as Spectator Sport: A Historical Perspective" We reflexively regard inclusive elections as the quintessential instrument of modern political life and the universal index of democratic legitimacy. But the spectacle of mass two-party competition that has dominated (and in some ways distinguished) U.S. electoral politics since the middle decades of the nineteenth century has relied upon and reinforced feelings of engagement and investment that warrant closer examination and thicker description. Drawn from a forthcoming book on the subject due out next year from Prickly Paradigm Press and ongoing research on American electoral culture in the 1840s, this lecture reconsiders the history of partisan political feeling in the United States alongside the evolution of partisan sports spectatorship. The talk will be followed by a lively Q&A.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Adam Steinbrenner | Seeing like a plant: immune recognition and signaling by cell surface receptors
events.description: Plants sense extracellular cues through several hundred cell surface receptors. The most rapidly evolving group of receptors is the leucine-rich repeat receptor-like proteins (RLPs), which transduce immune signals as a bipartite receptor complex with the adapter SOBIR1. In recent years many new examples of immunogenic patterns detected by specific RLPs have been described, highlighting their versatility as immune sensing modules. I will discuss unique features of the RLP family that mediate recognition and signaling functions. For recognition, RLPs encode an extracellular island domain, which allosterically couples ligand binding to co-receptor recruitment. For signaling, RLPs lack a kinase domain typical of most receptors, but the short cytoplasmic tail domain can encode signaling through different defense pathways. For both recognition and signaling functions, I will describe new insights from our study of Inceptin Receptor (INR), which detects caterpillar-derived peptide elicitors and evolved 28 mya in a single subtribe of legumes. Since both island and tail domains are small (~10-60 aa) shared features of all RLPs, they may represent modular, editable handles to engineer plant immune systems.

events.title: Stuart Russell: The purpose of AI
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Time: 12:00pm Location: 101 Weill hall Speaker: Stuart Russell Affiliation: Computer Science, UC Berkeley (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/stuart-russell)

events.title: IPSR Colloquium: Panel: "Minds in the Loop: Psychology and AI Alignment"
events.location: Room 1102 Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA 94704, USA
events.description: Brad Knox, Brian Christian, and Marjan SharifiMinds in the Loop: Psychology and AI Alignment Moderator: Bill Thompson, Assistant Professor of Psychology, UC Berkeley Wednesday, Oct 21, 2026 12:10 pm to 1:30 pm Room 1102, 2121 Berkeley WayBrad KnoxResearch Associate Professor of Computer Science, UT AustinBuilding RLHF Around Psychological Models of Human Preference Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) algorithms assume a preference probability function, a mapping from a human's desires to preference labels, given a pair of options. This mapping is effectively a psychological model of how humans form preferences and is used in RLHF to invert a preference dataset to infer the hidden desires of humans. In the context of general decision-making (e.g., robotics) and LLMs: I will discuss the accuracy of various psychological models of preference, the impact of the RLHF assuming different psychological models than those used to generate the preference labels, and how designers can help people conform more to a chosen psychological model. Along the way, I will consider what type of reward function can be drawn from different preference probability functions, impacting when learning superhuman performance is possible. Brian ChristianResearch Fellow, Center for Human-Compatible AI, UC BerkeleyReward Models Are Not Blank Slates, and LLMs Can't Un-Know: Cognitive Science at Two Steps of the Alignment PipelineAligning language models with human preferences runs through two objects that psychology has tools to study: the reward model (RM), trained to stand in for human judgment, and the deployed language model (LLM), which must reason about its own. I first consider RMs as artifacts of human value. Exhaustively scoring every token in a model's vocabulary against value-laden prompts reveals that leading open-weight RMs exhibit framing and mere-exposure effects like those seen in humans, and devalue identity-group terms relative to human baselines. Using validated psycholinguistic corpora, I show that RMs inherit systematic "Big Two" (agency/communion) preferences from their pretrained base models, which preference data narrows but does not erase – raising the question of how faithfully RMs can stand in as proxies for human preferences. I then turn to deployed LLMs, showing that, like people asked to imagine they didn't know a biasing fact, LLMs cannot simulate their own counterfactual judgments, and prompting them to try can backfire. Unlike people, however, they can converse with their own counterfactual selves – eliminating demographic bias, sharply reducing sycophancy, and exposing cases where a model knowingly overrides its own unbiased verdict. Marjan SharifiVisiting Scholar, University of California, Berkeley; Marie Sk��odowska-Curie Global Fellow, Cognitive Science and Psycholinguistic Lab, École normale supérieure and Institute of Personality and Social Research, UC BerkeleyReimagining Alignment Through Insights from Human Creative ProcessesWhen AI engineers think about human-AI alignment they tend to focus on the technical system and how well the AI can extrapolate and satisfy human values and preferences. What is missing is a process level alignment where the system would account for the exploratory processes by which we generate preferences, values and ultimately meaning. I will draw from mind-wandering research which illustrates the importance of balancing evaluative and exploratory thought for generating insight, how awareness and consideration of our thought processes (meta-cognition) can come to transform wander into wonder, and the role temporality plays in contextualizing meaning. Beyond simply accounting for, this talk will demonstrate how these systems can come to support human meaning making and thus eudaimonia. Central to this is proposing metrics of engagement based on how well the AI system supports these wellbeing factors related to our capacity to be curious and generate meaning for ourselves. Thus reimagining alignment through how it supports human creativity.

Panelist bios:Brad Knox (https://bradknox.net/) is a Research Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Texas at Austin. He is visiting UC Berkeley's Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI) for the 2026–2027 academic year. His research centers on the human side of reinforcement learning, and he's received multiple best paper awards on this topic. Currently, he primarily focuses on how humans can specify reward functions that are aligned with their interests, and he also works on interactive machine learning and AI companionship. Brad co-leads UT Austin's AI+Human Objectives Initiative (AHOI (https://sites.utexas.edu/ahoi/)), a faculty group and talk series focused on AI alignment and safety. His dissertation on the TAMER framework comprised pioneering work on human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and it won the 2012 best dissertation award for the UT Austin Department of Computer Science. Before his current role at UT Austin, he was a postdoc at the MIT Media Lab; founded and sold his toy robotics startup Bots Alive (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/bradknox/bots-alive-robots-that-play-and-find-their-way); co-led the Bosch Learning Agents Lab at UT Austin; and was a Senior Research Scientist at Google.Brian Christian (https://brianchristian.org/) is a computer scientist, cognitive scientist, and bestselling author whose work explores the human implications of computing. His work as a researcher spans AI alignment and computational cognitive science, and has appeared in journals from PNAS to Dædalus to Cognitive Science, and at conferences from ICLR to COLM to FAccT to NeurIPS. He completed his PhD at Oxford's Human Information Processing Lab, supported by the Clarendon Scholarship; his thesis received a Letter of Commendation from the Medical Sciences Division and an examination prize from Lincoln College. His research has been discussed in Nature, The New York Times, The Guardian, and Wired. His books include The Alignment Problem (https://brianchristian.org/the-alignment-problem/), Algorithms to Live By (https://brianchristian.org/algorithms-to-live-by/) (coauthored with Tom Griffiths), and The Most Human Human (https://brianchristian.org/the-most-human-human/). He is a Research Fellow at the Center for Human-Compatible AI (https://humancompatible.ai/) at UC Berkeley.Marjan Sharifi (https://www.marjansharifi.com/) is a cognitive scientist who investigates how artistic practices and interactive technologies shape our cognitive processes and emotions. She draws from the fields of neuroscience, psychology and philosophy to examine human-AI alignment through the human lens. She earned her PhD in the department of social neuroscience at the Max Planck Institute (MPI) for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences, training with the late Jonathan Smallwood, one of the leaders of mind-wandering research. One of the most formative experiences in her career came when she transitioned from working at the MPI to become the first scientist hired at the Berlin studio of the globally renowned artist Olafur Eliasson. By bringing together art and science, she learned to measure experiences that have not yet reached conscious awareness but still shape the world models we build. She now applies these insights as a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Global Fellow at the ENS in Paris and UC Berkeley, investigating the possibility of reverse engineering creative thinking by guiding where and how people mind-wander. As a research advisor to Princeton's Safe Robotics Lab (a position which grew from her collaborations with UC Berkeley's Center for Human-Compatible AI), where she co-developed a successful Coefficient Giving grant on how metacognition can make AI reasoning more sound and aligned. As an educator across universities in Europe and the US since 2017. Also as a mother, a friend and a daughter of a Persian poetry scholar and a NASA engineer, which is where her bridge-building skills developed.Bill Thompson (https://billdthompson.github.io/) is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, where he directs the Computational Cognitive Science Laboratory (https://ccs-ucb.github.io/). His work examines fundamental questions about intelligence at the intersection of human cognition and artificial intelligence, with a focus on social intelligence. You can learn more about his work in this short essay (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ade3128). events.title: Zonian Archaeology: Sovereign Soil and territorializing American Identity in the Archaeology of Panamá
events.description: This talk will take place in person at the ARF and on Zoom.Register for online attendance here. (https://bit.ly/ARFtalks-2627) About: From 1903 to 1979, the United States operated the Panama Canal Zone as ostensibly a sovereign entity. Developing housing, offices, schools, and a police force to govern this area, the United States created the imperial conditions for a new identity of American citizens to emerge—reffering to themselves as "Zonians" Americans in Panamá lived in a state within a state, defined by different access to resources, liberties, and ways of building and maintaining their heritage. Among the many clubs and societies established within the zone included an amateur archaeology group, called the Archaeological Society of Panamá. In operation from 1948-1969, this group conducted excavations both within and outside of the Panamá Canal Zone, with special exhibitions mounted in the Panama Canal Zone's Library and Museum (now dissolved), open to all Zonians. This paper argues that the Archaeological Society of Panamá and associated historical societies enfolded Panamanian pasts into a growing sense of American heritage, revising the boundaries of American sovereignty to include the archaeological subsoil and its pre-Columbian designs. Through archival sources and object analysis at the Panama Canal Archives and the Hearst Museum collections, a story emerges of how Zonians renegotiated Panama's proprietary past for a more expansive definition of ancient American heritage.

events.title: Moving Ideas into Action in a Shifting Policy Landscape: A Symposium Marking Twenty Years of the Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment
events.description: Join Berkeley Law's Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment (CLEE) for a symposium marking the research center's 20th anniversary. Berkeley Law established the Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment (CLEE) in 2006 – a time when California was launching bold, world-leading policies to address climate and environmental issues. At the same time, the federal government was walking back from its commitments and trying to limit the State's authority. Fast forward twenty years and the policy landscape looks similar, albeit much more dire – both in the urgency of the climate crisis and the scale of federal rollbacks and attacks on state action. Over the past twenty years, CLEE has honed its focus and expertise in this shifting and dynamic policy landscape. A large portion of CLEE's work has focused at the subnational level and has resulted in significant contributions from the local to global scale. This half-day symposium, marking the 20th anniversary of CLEE, welcomes new and long-time friends and partners of CLEE to discuss the challenges, impacts, and significance of environmental law and policy scholarship and how to make a difference in a dynamic policy landscape. Speakers include: Senator Henry Stern '09 (CA District 27) Professor Dan Farber, Founding Faculty Director of CLEE Rick Frank, Founding Executive Director of CLEE Rachel Morello-Frosch, Inaugural Associate Provost of Energy, Climate, and the Environment, UC Berkeley The symposium will be held from 2:00–5:00 p.m., and followed by a reception with drinks and hors d'oeuvres. We are grateful to our event sponsors, Brownstein, Nossaman, Orrick, Sheppard, The Tomblin Family Foundation, Willis Towers Watson, and Wilson Sonsini. We encourage you to RSVP (https://20yearsofclee.eventbrite.com/) at your earliest convenience due to limited space. Please email Maia Baltzley at maia.baltzley@berkeley.edu within 7 days of the symposium if you will need an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.), or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate.

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: Sharp localization and gaps for quasiperiodic operators with monotone potentials
events.description: Speaker: Tom Stoiber, UCBFor quasi-periodic one-dimensional Schrödinger operators a central conjecture is that localization at a given energy is determined purely by competition between the Lyapunov exponent and the irrationality exponent of the frequency. Among the classes of sampling functions for which this sharp transition is known are anti-Lipschitz monotone potentials, as was proven in a series of works by Jitomirskaya and Kachkovskiy. For monotone potentials the sampling functions increase between periodic jumps, and the anti-Lipschitz condition imposes a uniform positive lower bound on their rate of increase. In recent work we managed to substantially weaken this assumption and proved the sharp transition for any nonconstant C^1-monotone sampling function and even small non-monotone perturbations thereof. Some consequences of this include Cantor spectrum. In this talk, I will introduce sharp arithmetic localization and outline the main ideas of our proof. The results presented are joint work with Svetlana Jitomirskaya and Netanel Levi.

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History
events.description: Salt lakes are some of the world's most extraordinary ecosystems, but nearly all of them―from the Great Salt Lake to the Aral Sea��are drying up, a harbinger of dust storms, rising sea levels, and worsening human health. Caroline Tracey's book Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History, a hybrid work of memoir and geographic research, spans the American West, Mexico, Argentina, Kazakhstan and beyond, documenting salt lakes, their loss, and the efforts underway to save them, as well as Tracey's relationships to the lakes. In this talk she will describe the making of the book, including how it draws on her training in geographic methods and on additional creative sources such as Mormon diaries, Soviet realist novels, Australian Aboriginal paintings, and techniques of memoir and the personal essay. Caroline Tracey is the author of Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History (W.W. Norton, 2026). After receiving her PhD in Geography from the University of California, Berkeley, she became an independent writer and journalist specializing in the Southwestern US, Mexico, and their borderlands. Her work has appeared in numerous publications and has received a Fulbright fellowship, the Waterston Prize for Desert Writing, an Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writer's Grant, and a Creative Capital State of the Arts Award.

events.title: Descriptive Set Theory Working Seminar: Failure of the $L^1$ pointwise ergodic theorem
events.description: Speaker: MohammedSaid Alhalimi, UC BerkeleyThe goal of this talk is to explore some concrete examples of the failure of the ergodic theorem. I will review the work of Nevo and Stein which establishes pointwise ergodic theorems of $F_2$ actions for $L^p$ functions ($p1$) using spherical averaging operators. Following Tao (2015), I will introduce an example of a measure-preserving system with an $L^1$ function whose sequence of averages is unbounded thereby witnessing the failure of $L^1$ pointwise ergodic theorems for $F_2$ actions.

events.title: EECS Colloquium | Space Exploration at Berkeley, and the NASA Psyche mission: Journey to a Metal World
events.description: The Berkeley Space Sciences Lab has been flying successful space missions for over 60 years. We have some astounding projects to share, and a faculty affiliate program. The newest mission to join SSL is the NASA Psyche mission. Humankind has never visited a space object with a metal surface, and the spacecraft will arrive at this strange asteroid in just three years. I'll explain the science, the engineering, and the human story of planning, competing, building, and flying this mission. Lindy Elkins-Tanton is a professor and director of the Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory and lead of the NASA Psyche mission. Previously, she was a Vice President at Arizona State University, a director at the Carnegie Institution for Science, and faculty at MIT. Asteroid (8252) Elkins-Tanton is named for her, as is the mineral elkinstantonite. She is a member of the National Academy of Sciences. Elkins-Tanton received her B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. from MIT. She is the author of Mission Ready: How to Build Teams that Perform Under Pressure and A Portrait of the Scientist as a Young Woman.

events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Reese Pathak: Revisiting statistical principles for risk minimization
events.description: Abstract: Minimizing a loss over a set of data points is ubiquitous in data science. A complete understanding of which loss to minimize, however, is lacking. This talk focuses on an extremely simple model: estimating an unknown mean corrupted by Gaussian noise. An intuitive guess is that minimizing square loss (equivalently, maximizing the likelihood) over the parameter space would be the best estimator possible. Counterintuitively, this is suboptimal in general. Embarrassingly, the reasons for why this occurs are not fully understood! I will explain some reasons why this can happen, what can be done about it, and some related results around this theme. Based on several papers, joint with Liviu Aoloritei (UC Berkeley), Cong Ma (U. Chicago), Michael I. Jordan (UC Berkeley/INRIA), Annie Ulichney (UC Berkeley), and Nikita Zhivotovskiy (UC Berkeley).
